chapter: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
title: Beverly Peer fills in; Joe's later crashes and death
summary: Beverly Peer substitutes while Joe heals, Joe keeps driving recklessly, and he eventually dies in a car crash.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: But during the interim of that, we got another bass player who was a New Yorker that was out of that same group of bass players that seemed to be all friends and buddies or comrades or whatever. His name was Beverly Peer. Beverly for the past few years has been the bassist with the great Bobby Short, national and international fame, known greatly on the

East Side as one of the I guess biggest personalities in that particular field of that kind of entertainment. Anyway, Beverly came with us, and he remained with us until Joe was well enough to come back.

Somehow, the accident didn't seem to change Joe's driving habits at all. Because coming out of the hospital, it seems as if he was in Washington D.C. here, and within a matter of weeks or months that he'd been back to work, he was driving down Florida Avenue here... I wasn't there, but someone told that he had hit five cars on his way... And this is right in the city.

But anyway, it was a rather tragic thing, because Joe was really one of the finest guys you'd want to know. He was a very intellectual person. He knew a little bit about everything. He spoke French very well. And all of the ladies was crazy about him, because he was a very classy guy. He was one of these guys that did everything proper but drive a car. And the results of all of this was his death a few years ago. I think it was the same year that Duke Ellington died. He was a member of the band. And his death was in an automobile accident outside of New York.
But as in all of these kind of things, there are tragedies, and then there are good times, you know.
